title: Trench Soil Classification: Type A, B, and C
summary: Soil type decides which protective system a trench needs. A competent person classifies the soil by a visual check and by tests, and repeats it when conditions change.
talking_points: Trenching kills about 40 construction workers a year. One cubic yard of soil can weigh as much as a car, about 3,000 pounds.
A protective system is required for trenches 5 feet deep or more, unless dug in stable rock. Trenches under 5 feet need one if a competent person sees signs of a possible cave-in.

A competent person determines the soil type and must inspect the excavation every day and when conditions change. Excavations deeper than 20 feet need a protective system approved by a professional engineer.

Type A is the most stable: cohesive, 1.5 tons per square foot or more, like clay. Type B is between 0.5 and 1.5 tons per square foot, like angular gravel and silt. Type C is the least stable: 0.5 or less, granular soils like sand and gravel, and any soil with water seeping through it.

Soil cannot be Type A if it is fissured, was disturbed before, has water seeping through it, or is near vibration such as heavy traffic or pile drivers. A trench can cut through more than one soil type.
Do a visual check first. Does the soil come out in clumps (cohesive) or as granules? Look for vibration, old utility lines, seepage, and cracks or crumbling on the wall.

Tests: the plasticity test (roll a thread 1/8 inch thick and 2 inches long). The thumb test (thumb sinks in: Type A only with great effort, Type B to the thumbnail, Type C all the way). The pocket penetrometer (may give false readings with rocks or pebbles). Use more than one test.
Take typical samples from a fresh pile or the wall, take more as the trench gets deeper, and test soon, because results change as soil dries.
site_hazards_to_check: Fissured, cracked, or crumbling trench walls
Vibration from traffic, equipment, or pile driving near the trench
Previously disturbed soil, such as around utility lines
Soil type not tested or not written down for this trench
Trench 5 feet or deeper with no protective system
discussion_questions: Who is the competent person for this trench, and what soil type did they find?
What did the visual check and the tests show, and how often will we check again?
What changed today, such as rain or nearby traffic, that could change the soil type?
